newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Is notes demand behind tight Belgian money market?.
newsitem.headline: Is notes demand behind tight Belgian money market?.

text.p: Is an explosion in the amount of bank notes in circulation in Belgium due to demand from the public partly behind high Belgian money market yields?
In the first half of 1997 the volume of notes in circulation rose by three percent to 482.5 billion Belgian francs. That rise followed an unusually high 4.2 percent rise in 1996.
In the week to Monday, as one would expect at the start of the holiday season, the rise continued, the central bank's weekly balance sheet statement published on Wednesday showed.
Belgian three-month deposits were at around 3.37/42 percent on Friday, some 35 basis points over similar German yields.
A rise in notes in circulation means money has been withdrawn from bank accounts and is no longer available for re-lending, thus tightening money market conditions.
In its weekly statement the National Bank of Belgium said it added liquidity to offset just such an effect.
One senior official confirmed such movements are taken into account in money market operations.

However, the central bank has yet to explain for the increase. In its 1996 annual report it noted only the traditional "seasonal fluctuations" in notes demand were "different in some respects" to previous years.

One official said, however, the reason was probably the virtual absence of inflation and historically low interest rates. Belgian inflation was 1.74 percent in June, little changed from year-earlier levels.

"At times of high inflation and high interest rates you normally have a move to deposits," he noted. "It's possible that in 1997 other accidental movements took place but I think a large part of the increase can be explained by inflation going down."
